title: Mahashivratri: what to wear and the meaning of rudraksha
description: Colours, outfits and jewellery that suit Mahashivratri temple visits and night-long jagran, plus why rudraksha is traditionally worn on this night.
intro: For Mahashivratri, most people choose simple, comfortable clothes in white, cream, light green or saffron, and keep jewellery light, with a rudraksha mala as the one devotional piece. The festival involves fasting, long temple queues and often a night-long jagran, so practicality matters as much as looks. Here is how to dress for each part of the day, and why rudraksha holds such a special place on this night.

sections.heading: Plan for a long night, not just a puja
paragraphs: Unlike many festivals, Mahashivratri is observed mainly through the night. Devotees visit temples for abhishek, stay awake for jagran with bhajans, and many fast through the day. You may be standing in a queue for an hour, sitting cross-legged on a temple floor, or offering water and milk to the Shivling. Dress for all of that: breathable fabric, a hemline that will not trail in water, and footwear that is easy to slip off at the temple entrance.

It also helps to carry a small cloth bag. Into it go your phone, a little cash for flowers and bel leaves, a handkerchief to dry your hands after abhishek, and a pouch in case you want to take off any jewellery inside the temple. Packing light means you can move through the queue without juggling things.

sections.heading: Colours people usually prefer
paragraphs: There is no single prescribed colour, and customs differ by region. Still, a few choices come up again and again:
list: White and off-white: linked with Shiva's ash-smeared, ascetic form and with purity. The most common choice in many temples.
Light green: associated with bel leaves, which are offered to Shiva, and popular in North India.
Saffron and orange: a traditional colour of renunciation and devotion.
Light blue: sometimes chosen as a nod to Shiva as Neelkanth, the blue-throated one.
Black: some families avoid it on festival days, while others have no such rule. If you are unsure, pick another colour.

sections.heading: Outfit ideas that work
paragraphs: For women, a cotton or chanderi suit with a light dupatta is the easiest option for a temple visit. A simple cotton or linen saree works well for an evening puja at home or a jagran in a community hall. Keep the dupatta pinned, since you will bend often to offer water or flowers.

For men, a white or pastel cotton kurta with pyjama or straight trousers is the classic choice. A short kurta over jeans is perfectly fine for a quick temple visit on the way home from work. In cold northern cities, add a plain shawl rather than a heavy jacket so you can wrap and unwrap it easily through the night.

sections.heading: Why rudraksha is worn on this night
paragraphs: Rudraksha is the bead most closely tied to Shiva. Its name joins Rudra, a name of Shiva, with aksha, often translated as eye or tear, and a well-known story says rudraksha trees grew from Shiva's tears after a long meditation. Since Mahashivratri is regarded as the great night of Shiva, many devotees believe it is an especially good time to start wearing a new mala, or to chant on an existing one through the jagran.

Some people chant Om Namah Shivaya 108 times on their mala; others simply wear it as a mark of devotion. Both are common, and neither depends on owning a rare or expensive bead. A simple five mukhi mala, or a [rudraksha chain mala with a Shiva or Trishul pendant](/divine), is how most people take part.

sections.heading: Jewellery for temple visits and abhishek
paragraphs: Crowded temples and pouring water call for a lighter hand with jewellery. A few practical rules help:
list: Wear one devotional piece, such as a rudraksha mala, and keep everything else minimal.
Choose studs or small jhumkas over long earrings that can catch in a dupatta or a crowd.
Avoid heavy bangles if you will be pouring water or milk; they slip and get wet.
If your mala has a gold-plated pendant, tuck it inside your kurta during abhishek and wipe it dry later.
Leave valuable or sentimental pieces at home for very crowded temples.

sections.heading: For a puja at home
paragraphs: At home you have more freedom. A cotton silk saree with small [Kundan or Meenakari earrings](/women/earrings) and a rudraksha chain looks festive without being fussy. Men can wear the mala over a kurta so the pendant shows. If you are hosting a jagran, choose clothes you can sit in for hours, and keep a cardigan or shawl nearby for the early hours of the morning, when it can get surprisingly cold.

faq.q: Which colour should I wear on Mahashivratri?
faq.a: White, cream, light green and saffron are popular. There is no single rule, and some families avoid black on festival days.

faq.q: Is Mahashivratri a good day to start wearing rudraksha?
faq.a: Many devotees believe so, as it is the great night of Shiva. Others start on any Monday. Follow your family's custom.

faq.q: Can I wear jewellery while fasting?
faq.a: Yes. Fasting rules apply to food, not jewellery. Most people simply keep it light and comfortable for the long night.
